title: Resource And Population Dynamics In An Agent-environment Interaction Model
authors: Gaston Briozzo, Gustavo J. Sibona, And Fernando Peruani
abstract:
Author(s): Gaston Briozzo, Gustavo J. Sibona, and Fernando Peruani

In any ecosystem, the conditions of the environment and the characteristics of the species that inhabit it are entangled, coevolving in space and time. We introduce a model that couples active agents with a dynamic environment, interpreted as a nutrient source. Agents are persistent random walkers t…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064406] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper models the coevolution of active agents and a dynamic nutrient environment, focusing on population dynamics and resource consumption.
motivation: To understand how species characteristics and environmental conditions coevolve in ecosystems, using a minimal model of active agents and a diffusing resource.
method: The authors introduce a model where agents perform persistent random walks and consume a locally diffusing nutrient, with agent reproduction and death coupled to resource availability.
result: The model exhibits complex spatiotemporal patterns, including traveling waves and localized clusters, depending on agent motility and resource diffusion rates.
conclusion: The coupling between agent behavior and resource dynamics leads to emergent phenomena relevant to ecological systems, but the model is purely classical and not connected to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Chromatic Percolation In Two-dimensional Multitype Particle Systems With Extended-range Homotypic Repulsion
authors: Tingting Yin, Yan Sui, Xueying Yuan, And Xian Kong
abstract:
Author(s): Tingting Yin, Yan Sui, Xueying Yuan, and Xian Kong

Cells in many tissues repel like neighbors over extended ranges, yet standard jamming models ignore this diversity. We introduce chromatic percolation—the percolation of like-type particles driven by extended-range homotypic repulsion in multitype assemblies—and map its relation to mechanical jammin…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065412] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: Introduces chromatic percolation in multitype particle systems with extended-range homotypic repulsion, linking percolation to mechanical jamming.
motivation: Standard jamming models ignore diversity in cell-cell repulsion ranges; this work aims to understand how homotypic repulsion drives percolation and jamming in multitype assemblies.
method: Develops a chromatic percolation model for two-dimensional multitype particle systems with extended-range homotypic repulsion, analyzed via simulations and theoretical mapping.
result: Finds that extended-range homotypic repulsion can induce percolation of like-type particles, which correlates with mechanical jamming transitions.
conclusion: Chromatic percolation provides a framework to connect percolation and jamming in diverse biological and soft matter systems.

title: Contrasting Impurity-induced Magnetism And Dynamics In $2H\text{−}{\mathrm{MoTe}}_{2}$
authors: Jonas A. Krieger, Igor P. Rusinov, Sourabh Barua, Aris Chatzichristos, Jared Croese, Derek Fujimoto, Stefan Holenstein, Victoria L. Karner, Ryan M. L. Mcfadden, John O. Ticknor, W. [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023316] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies impurity-induced magnetism and dynamics in 2H-MoTe2 using β-NMR, finding no magnetic signature for 8Li unlike muons.
motivation: To understand the behavior of interstitial impurities in transition metal dichalcogenides and their magnetic properties.
method: β-detected nuclear magnetic resonance (β-NMR) is used to probe 8Li implanted near the surface of 2H-MoTe2.
result: 8Li shows no induced magnetism, contrasting with muon results, and the spin-lattice relaxation reveals two distinct dynamic regimes.
conclusion: The absence of magnetism for 8Li suggests a different interaction mechanism compared to muons, highlighting the role of impurity species in local magnetic properties.

title: Machine-learning-guided Discovery Of Kagome Superconductors ${\mathrm{YRu}}_{3}{\mathrm{B}}_{2}$ And ${\mathrm{LuRu}}_{3}{\mathrm{B}}_{2}$
authors: Rose Albu Mustaf, Sajilesh K. P., Sanu Mishra, Junze Deng, Yi Jiang, Kaja H. Hiorth, Eeli O. Lamponen, Martin Gutierrez-Amigo, Päivi Törmä, Miguel A. L. Marques, B. Andrei Bernevig, And Emilia Morosan
abstract:
Author(s): Rose Albu Mustaf, Sajilesh K. P., Sanu Mishra, Junze Deng, Yi Jiang, Kaja H. Hiorth, Eeli O. Lamponen, Martin Gutierrez-Amigo, Päivi Törmä, Miguel A. L. Marques, B. Andrei Bernevig, and Emilia Morosan

tldr: Machine learning and first-principles calculations predict and experimentally discover two new kagome superconductors.
motivation: To discover new kagome superconductors using machine-learning-accelerated high-throughput screening combined with first-principles calculations.
method: Machine learning models trained on known materials predict candidate kagome compounds; first-principles calculations validate electronic structure; experimental synthesis and characterization confirm superconductivity.
result: Two new kagome superconductors, YRu3B2 and LuRu3B2, are discovered and characterized.
conclusion: Machine learning can accelerate the discovery of novel superconductors in kagome lattices.

title: Observation Of Surface Ferromagnons In The Axion-insulating Phase Of The Antiferromagnetic Topological Insulator ${\mathrm{EuSn}}_{2}{\mathrm{As}}_{2}$
authors: Mamoun Hemmida, Santanu Pakhira, David C. Johnston, And Hans-Albrecht Krug von Nidda
abstract:
Author(s): Mamoun Hemmida, Santanu Pakhira, David C. Johnston, and Hans-Albrecht Krug von Nidda

We report the study of spin dynamics of [MATH] in the antiferromagnetic axion topological insulator [MATH] by means of antiferromagnetic resonance at 9.34 GHz. Below the Néel temperature ([MATH]), two types of resonance modes, the conventiona…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023309] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports antiferromagnetic resonance measurements in the topological insulator EuSn2As2, observing surface ferromagnons in the axion-insulating phase.
motivation: To study spin dynamics and surface magnetic excitations in a topological insulator with antiferromagnetic order, which is relevant to axion electrodynamics.
method: Electron spin resonance (ESR) at 9.34 GHz was used to measure antiferromagnetic resonance modes below the Néel temperature.
result: Two resonance modes were observed: conventional antiferromagnetic resonance and a surface ferromagnon mode, indicating surface magnetic order.
conclusion: The surface ferromagnon mode is a signature of the axion-insulating phase, providing insight into the interplay between magnetism and topology.

title: Confinement And Finite-range Effects In A Quasi-two-dimensional Gas Of Fermionic Dimers
authors: Giovanni Midei, Jordi Boronat, And Grigory E. Astrakharchik
abstract:
Author(s): Giovanni Midei, Jordi Boronat, and Grigory E. Astrakharchik

A study of a gas of fermionic dimers in a quasi-two-dimensional geometry induced by strong harmonic confinement in one direction is presented. Fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo calculations are used to quantify the effects of confinement and finite interaction range on the equation of state and density profiles, with the results benchmarked against analytical theories.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022051] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: A Monte Carlo study of fermionic dimers in a quasi-2D geometry, focusing on confinement and finite-range effects on the equation of state.
motivation: To understand how strong confinement and finite interaction range affect the properties of a gas of fermionic dimers, relevant to ultracold atomic systems.
method: Fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo simulations are used to compute the equation of state and density profiles, benchmarked against analytical theories.
result: Quantifies the effects of confinement and finite range, showing deviations from simple analytical models.
conclusion: The study provides benchmarks for future experiments and theoretical models of quasi-2D fermionic dimer gases.

title: Manifold-based Transformation Of Probability Distributions: Application To The Inverse Problem Of Reconstructing Distributions From Experimental Data
authors: Tomotaka Oroguchi, Rintaro Inoue, And Masaaki Sugiyama
abstract:
Author(s): Tomotaka Oroguchi, Rintaro Inoue, and Masaaki Sugiyama

Information geometry is a mathematical framework that elucidates the manifold structure of the probability distribution space (p space), providing a systematic approach to transforming probability distributions (PDs). In this study, we utilized information geometry to address the inverse problems as…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023291] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses information geometry to transform probability distributions for solving inverse problems in experimental data reconstruction.
motivation: The authors aim to address the inverse problem of reconstructing probability distributions from experimental data, which is a common challenge in data analysis.
method: They apply information geometry, specifically the manifold structure of probability distribution spaces, to systematically transform distributions and solve the inverse problem.
result: The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the manifold-based transformation approach for reconstructing distributions from experimental data.
conclusion: Information geometry provides a powerful framework for inverse problems involving probability distributions, with potential applications in various experimental fields.

title: Revealing Charge Anisotropies In Metal Compounds Via High-purity X-ray Polarimetry
authors: Lena Scherthan, Juliusz A. Wolny, Isabelle Faus, Olaf Leupold, Kai S. Schulze, Sebastian Höfer, Robert Loetzsch, Berit Marx-Glowna, Christopher E. Anson, Annie K. Powell, Ingo Uschmann, Hans-Christian Wille, Gerhard G. Paulus, Volker Schünemann, And Ralf Röhlsberger

method: The authors employ polarization-resolved nuclear forward scattering (PR-NFS) of synchrotron radiation at the 14.4 keV nuclear resonance of 57Fe to measure linear polarization of hard X-rays.
result: The technique reveals charge anisotropies with high selectivity in metal-containing complexes.
conclusion: High-purity X-ray polarimetry is a powerful tool for probing electronic structure, but the work is purely experimental materials characterization.

This representation manifold…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023281] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical learning in asymmetric recurrent neural networks, focusing on the emergence of stable configuration manifolds.
motivation: To understand how asymmetric interactions and self-couplings in recurrent neural networks can lead to complex dynamical behavior and learning.
method: The authors analyze recurrent neural networks with asymmetric interactions, incorporating self-couplings or sparse excitatory intermodule connections, and study the resulting manifold of stable configurations.
result: They demonstrate that such networks can develop a densely connected manifold of dynamically accessible stable configurations, which may facilitate learning.
conclusion: Asymmetric recurrent neural networks with appropriate couplings can exhibit rich dynamical properties relevant for learning, but the work is primarily in machine learning and statistical physics, not directly related to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Are Neural Networks Collision Resistant?
authors: Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, And Riccardo Zecchina
abstract:
Author(s): Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, and Riccardo Zecchina

A study of the computational complexity of finding collisions in a simple one-layer neural network shows that efficient algorithms fail to find collisions, a result of direct relevance for the definition of new cryptographic protocols based on machine-learning models.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021051] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of finding collisions in a simple one-layer neural network, showing that efficient algorithms fail, which is relevant for cryptography based on machine learning.
motivation: To understand whether neural networks can serve as collision-resistant hash functions for cryptographic protocols.
method: The authors analyze the computational complexity of finding collisions in a one-layer neural network using theoretical and algorithmic approaches.
result: Efficient algorithms are shown to fail in finding collisions, suggesting that such neural networks may be collision resistant.
conclusion: The findings are relevant for defining new cryptographic protocols based on machine-learning models.

motivation: To understand the interplay between polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational orders in a homo-ferro-rotational insulator.

title: Excitations Across The Equilibrium And Photoinduced “Hidden” States Of Magnetoresistive Manganites
authors: Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, And Jonathan Pelliciari
abstract:

motivation: To understand the nature of photoinduced hidden phases in strongly correlated electron systems, which may have implications for controlling material properties.
method: The authors use resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and other ultrafast techniques to probe excitations in Pr0.67Ca0.33MnO3 under equilibrium and photoexcited conditions.
result: They observe unique polaronic and phononic excitations in the photoinduced hidden phase that are absent in equilibrium.
conclusion: The hidden phase exhibits distinct lattice and electronic excitations, suggesting a novel state of matter that could be exploited for applications.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques (STM, TEM, atom-probe) for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three complementary real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors survey scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, highlighting cases where techniques are combined for a more complete defect picture.
result: The review demonstrates how these techniques can directly image and characterize disorder at the atomic scale in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space probes provides a comprehensive understanding of atomic-scale disorder, which is essential for tailoring semiconductor properties.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on collective motion in biological and soft matter systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors, with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, presenting a unified mathematical framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, distinct from neighbor-based alignment.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter that can be harnessed for designing new materials and robotic systems.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions used in electronic-structure calculations.
method: The paper reviews the ecosystem of software tools that generate and use Wannier functions, describing their interoperability and applications.
result: It catalogs the capabilities of various codes and their roles in computing properties like topological invariants and accurate integrations.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling a wide range of materials simulations.

title: Electron Spin Drift In Long-distance Plasma Wakefield Acceleration
authors: Ming Zeng And Dazhang Li Yilan Guo
abstract: Plasma based wakefield acceleration of polarized electron beams has recently attracted considerable research interest. Previous works have found the forced spin oscillation of electrons due to two-dimensional betatron oscillation in particle trajectory and discovered longitudinal depolarization mechanism in plasma wakefield. In this work, we present a three-dimensional analytical model for the electron spin dynamics and derive the evolution of polarization during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration. Our analysis reveals several phenomena including a transverse rotational spin drift leading to depolarization, a reversal of the drift frequency, and a consequent recovery of polarization. This work can offer guidance on future plasma-based accelerators for polarized electron beams.
tldr: This paper presents a three-dimensional analytical model for electron spin dynamics in plasma wakefield acceleration, focusing on spin drift and depolarization.
motivation: Polarized electron beams are important for high-energy physics, but spin dynamics in plasma wakefield accelerators are not well understood, especially over long distances.
method: The authors develop a 3D analytical model for electron spin evolution during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration, incorporating betatron oscillations and wakefield effects.
result: They discover a transverse rotational spin drift leading to depolarization, a reversal of drift frequency, and a subsequent recovery of polarization.
conclusion: The work provides guidance for designing future plasma-based accelerators that preserve electron beam polarization.

title: Structural Origin Of Line-tension Reversal In Nanoscale Wetting Of Water
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 19 June 2026;
tldr: This paper studies the structural origin of line-tension reversal in nanoscale wetting of water using simulations.
motivation: The microscopic origin of line tension at solid-liquid-gas boundaries is not well understood, and understanding it is important for nanoscale wetting phenomena.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations of water nanodroplets on solid surfaces are performed to analyze structural transitions and their effect on line tension.
result: Structural transitions in the water nanodroplets are found to cause a reversal of line tension, affecting wetting behavior.
conclusion: The study reveals that line tension is not constant but can change sign due to structural changes, which has implications for nanoscale wetting and related applications.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: A multi-step model involving surface defects, electrical stress, heating, and particle emission explains the onset of vacuum arcs.
conclusion: Improved understanding can guide the design of more robust accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe, and their properties provide crucial tests of nuclear physics under extreme conditions.
method: The paper reviews recent observational results from gravitational-wave detections of binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, comparing them to theoretical predictions of the nuclear equation of state.
result: The measurements constrain neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, and are compared to extrapolations of nuclear equation of state calculations.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine our understanding of dense matter, but the paper does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonance phenomena.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions in stars is crucial for stellar burning and element formation, but many reactions are difficult to measure directly due to low rates.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques for studying these reactions on Earth.
result: Summarizes the state-of-the-art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory and identifies new ideas for laboratory measurements.
conclusion: Quantum mechanical effects dominate stellar nuclear reactions, and continued theoretical and experimental efforts are needed to improve our understanding.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables noninvasive imaging millimeters to centimeters deep with high resolution, impacting biological and clinical research.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological imaging, but it is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Kinetic Solitary Electrostatic Structures In Collisionless Plasma: Phase-space Holes
abstract:
Author(s): I. H. Hutchinson

Plasma is usually taught to be a quasineutral gas of charged and neutral particles that exhibits collective behavior. However, satellites regularly observe solitary potential structures in space plasmas that are isolated positive or negative potential humps, called electron or ion holes. In the 1970s, laboratory observations were made of electron holes. This review presents an overview of the observation of these electrostatic structures and presents their origin and their stability, using analytic theory and simulations. The role of kinetically unstable velocity distributions is identified as a key driver.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045007] Published Tue Dec 10, 2024.
tldr: A review of solitary electrostatic structures (phase-space holes) in collisionless plasma, covering observations, theory, and simulations.
motivation: To understand the formation, stability, and role of electron and ion holes in space and laboratory plasmas.
method: Review of satellite observations, analytic theory, and particle-in-cell simulations.
result: Phase-space holes arise from kinetic instabilities and are stable over long times, affecting plasma transport.
conclusion: Kinetic solitary structures are ubiquitous in collisionless plasmas and are key to understanding non-equilibrium plasma phenomena.

motivation: To develop a practical, mild, and scalable method for introducing fluorine-containing functional groups into organic molecules, which are important in pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals.
method: The authors use an electrochemical approach with secondary amines, a fluoride source, and carbon disulfide under open-air conditions without solvent drying or inert atmosphere.
result: The method successfully produces thiocarbamoyl fluorides and N-trifluoromethyl amines in good yields with broad substrate scope.
conclusion: This electrochemical method offers a simple and divergent route to valuable fluorinated compounds, avoiding harsh reagents and conditions.

title: Structure Of The Nat10 Acetyltransferase And Mechanism Of tRNA Acetylation
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 June 2026;
tldr: This paper reports cryo-EM structures of the NAT10 acetyltransferase and elucidates its catalytic mechanism for tRNA acetylation.
motivation: NAT10 acetylation is linked to disease, but its catalytic mechanism was unclear.
method: Cryo-EM structures of Chaetomium thermophilum NAT10 in complex with a cytidine-CoA probe with and without ADP were determined.
result: The structures reveal the architecture of NAT10 and provide insights into its acetylation mechanism.
conclusion: The study advances understanding of NAT10 function and its role in disease.

title: Atf4 Coordinates Amino Acid And Nucleotide Synthesis With Selective Protein Translation To Ensure Proper Dna Replication Timing In Leukemia Cells
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 June 2026;
tldr: This paper studies the role of ATF4 in coordinating amino acid and nucleotide synthesis with translation of replication machinery to ensure proper DNA replication timing in leukemia cells.
motivation: Leukemia cells require accelerated biomass production to fuel DNA replication, and understanding the regulatory mechanisms could reveal therapeutic targets.
method: The authors used molecular biology techniques to investigate ATF4's function in leukemia cells, likely including gene expression analysis, protein translation assays, and DNA replication timing measurements.
result: ATF4 couples amino acid and nucleotide synthesis with selective translation of replication machinery, ensuring proper DNA replication timing.
conclusion: ATF4 is a key coordinator of metabolic and translational programs necessary for DNA replication in leukemia, suggesting potential therapeutic strategies.

title: Rapid Warming In South America During The Last Deglaciation
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 20 June 2026;
tldr: This paper presents a tropical temperature record from stalagmites in South America during the last deglaciation, linking temperature changes to atmospheric CO₂ and ocean circulation.
motivation: To reconstruct tropical temperature variations across the last deglaciation and understand their relationship with global climate forcings.
method: Stable isotope and trace element analysis of stalagmites from central-eastern South America, combined with U-Th dating.
result: The tropical temperature record shows rapid warming that broadly tracks atmospheric CO₂ and changes in ocean circulation.
conclusion: Tropical South America experienced rapid warming during the last deglaciation, driven by greenhouse gases and ocean circulation changes.

authors: Nabeen Bhusal, Simone Blasi, Martina Cataldi, Aleksandr Chatrchyan, Marco Gorghetto, And Géraldine Servant
abstract:

We compute for the first time baryon number violation at zero temperature from Higgs bubble collisions and find that it can be of the same order as that from thermal sphalerons in the symmetric phase at electroweak temperatures. We study the dependence of the rate of Chern-Simons number transitions …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 241803] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies baryon number violation from Higgs bubble collisions at zero temperature, a topic in high-energy physics beyond the Standard Model.
motivation: Baryon number violation is a key ingredient for understanding the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe, and this work explores a new mechanism at zero temperature.
method: The authors compute the rate of Chern-Simons number transitions during Higgs bubble collisions using numerical simulations and analytical estimates.
result: They find that baryon number violation from bubble collisions can be comparable to that from thermal sphalerons at electroweak temperatures.
conclusion: This mechanism could contribute to baryogenesis and should be considered in models of electroweak phase transitions.

conclusion: The results offer new constraints on hyperon-nucleon potentials and improve models of dense nuclear matter.

authors: Yue Qian, Yue Li, And Bo Li

[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 248402] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.

motivation: Understanding how controlled cracking sculpts tissues through biological regulation, contrasting with mechanical failure in engineering.
method: Develops a nonlinear peridynamic model incorporating cellular mechanosensing at multiple scales.
result: The model predicts spontaneous periodic fracture patterns in active tissues.
conclusion: Periodic fracture can be a biologically regulated process, not just a failure mode.

method: Data collected by the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer on the ISS over 13.5 years, with one million events analyzed in the GV to TV rigidity range.
result: Unique properties of the fluxes of phosphorus, chlorine, argon, potassium, and calcium are presented.
conclusion: The results contribute to the understanding of cosmic ray composition and propagation.

Scalar-mediated interactions may exist among neutrinos, dark matter particles, or between the two. Double [MATH]-decay experiments provide a powerful tool to probe such exotic interactions. Using [MATH] double [MATH]-decay data from PandaX-4T, we perform the first direct spectral search in th…

motivation: To probe exotic scalar-mediated interactions among neutrinos and dark matter particles using direct detection data.
method: Performs a spectral search in the double beta decay data from PandaX-4T to constrain scalar couplings.
result: Sets new limits on scalar-neutrino and scalar-dark-matter interactions.
conclusion: Double beta decay experiments are effective tools for probing such exotic interactions.

motivation: To parametrize and compute corrections to general relativity from higher-derivative interactions in a low-energy effective field theory.
method: Numerical methods are used to solve the modified field equations and compute corrections to the Kerr metric.
result: The leading-order corrections to the Kerr metric are obtained for all spins.
conclusion: The results provide a general and agnostic parametrization of corrections to general relativity from UV completion.

title: Observation Of The Radiative Decay ${D}_{s0}^{*}(2317{)}^{+}→{D}_{s}^{*+}γ$
abstract:

tldr: Observation of the radiative decay of an exotic meson, D_s0*(2317)+ → D_s*+ γ, providing insight into its internal structure.
motivation: The D_s0*(2317)+ meson has a debated structure; its radiative decay can reveal its nature.
method: Analysis of data from Belle and Belle II experiments to measure the decay rate and properties.
result: First observation of the radiative decay, with measured branching fraction and photon energy spectrum.
conclusion: The decay properties support the interpretation of D_s0*(2317)+ as a hadronic molecule or tetraquark state.

authors: Marie Labat, Susanne Schöbel, Amin Ghaith, Franziska Marie Herrmann, Maxwell Laberge, Eléonore Roussel, Ulrich Schramm, Patrick Ufer, Marie-Emmanuelle Couprie, And Arie Irman

The realization of compact laser-plasma accelerator (LPA) driven free electron lasers (FELs) has been attempted for nearly two decades, yet, difficult to overcome electron beam quality and stability issues prevented FEL lasing until recently. motivation: Laser-plasma accelerators can produce high-energy electron beams in compact setups, but beam quality issues have prevented FEL lasing until now.
method: The authors used a laser-plasma accelerator to generate electron beams and seeded them with an external laser to achieve high-gain FEL amplification.
result: They observed exponential growth of the FEL radiation, confirming lasing in the high-gain regime with good agreement between experiment and theory.
conclusion: This work demonstrates the feasibility of compact LPA-based FELs, opening the way for table-top X-ray sources.

title: Ablating Pellets For Areal Density Symmetry Control In Indirectly Driven Inertial Confinement Fusion Target Designs

tldr: This paper presents a method using ablating pellets to control areal density symmetry in indirectly driven inertial confinement fusion targets.
motivation: Asymmetry in compressed fusion fuel limits performance in ICF implosions; controlling areal density symmetry is crucial for achieving ignition.
method: The authors propose and simulate the use of ablating pellets placed strategically to modify the radiation drive and improve symmetry.
result: Simulations show that ablating pellets can effectively reduce areal density variations, leading to more symmetric implosions.
conclusion: Ablating pellets offer a practical approach to symmetry control in ICF, potentially improving ignition performance.

title: Tangential Forces Govern The Viscous-Inertial Transition In Dense Frictional Suspensions

We present particle-resolved simulations of dense frictional suspensions undergoing the viscous-inertial transition using pressure-imposed rheology. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 248201] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the viscous-inertial transition in dense frictional suspensions using particle-resolved simulations, focusing on tangential forces.
motivation: Understanding the transition from viscous to inertial regimes in dense suspensions is important for industrial and natural processes, but the role of tangential forces was unclear.
method: Particle-resolved simulations with pressure-imposed rheology were performed, varying fluid viscosity, shear rate, and granular pressure to isolate the effect of tangential forces.
result: The transition occurs at a Stokes number close to the viscous-inertial crossover, and tangential forces are found to govern the transition.
conclusion: Tangential forces are key to the viscous-inertial transition in dense frictional suspensions, providing a mechanistic understanding.

title: Geometric Bookkeeping Guide To Feynman Integral Reduction And $ϵ$-Factorized Differential Equations
authors: Iris Bree, Federico Gasparotto, Antonela Matijašić, Pouria Mazloumi, Dmytro Melnichenko, Sebastian Pögel, Toni Teschke, Xing Wang, Stefan Weinzierl, Konglong Wu, And Xiaofeng Xu

tldr: This paper presents improvements in Feynman integral reduction and epsilon-factorized differential equations for high-energy physics calculations.
motivation: Feynman integral reduction is crucial for multi-loop scattering amplitudes in particle physics, but current methods are computationally expensive.
method: The authors propose three improvements: trivializing epsilon dependence in integration-by-parts identities, optimizing prefactor choices, and streamlining the reduction process.
result: The new approach simplifies the reduction and yields epsilon-factorized differential equations more efficiently.
conclusion: These improvements enhance the practicality of Feynman integral computations for precision phenomenology.

motivation: To improve the theoretical description of SBS in plasmas by incorporating more realistic collision dynamics.
method: Derives an analytic SBS gain coefficient from the Boltzmann equation with a generalized BGK collision term.
result: Obtains an expression for the SBS gain that accounts for velocity-dependent relaxation.
conclusion: The model provides a more accurate prediction of SBS behavior in collisional plasmas.

method: The authors compute quantum electrodynamic and recoil corrections analytically and incorporate proton structure corrections from hydrogen hyperfine splitting data.
result: They present a complete theory of the hyperfine splitting including all contributions above 1 ppm.
conclusion: The calculated hyperfine splitting provides a precise theoretical benchmark for future experiments.

method: Analyzes plume stretching in the trapped region of a reoriented potential mixer using dipole flow and numerical simulations.
result: Quantifies stretching and mixing efficiency in the trapped region under various reorientation protocols.

title: Bifurcations And Multistability In Inducible Three-gene Toggle Switch Networks
authors: Rebecca J. Rousseau And Rob Phillips

method: The authors analyze a mathematical model of a three-gene toggle switch network using bifurcation theory and numerical simulations.
result: They identify conditions for multistability and characterize bifurcation diagrams showing how the network switches between stable states.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the design principles of multistable gene circuits, with potential applications in synthetic biology.

This offset shapes an agent's ability to perceive and respond to neighbors, thereby impacting overall…

tldr: This paper studies how a fixed visual field offset affects collective motion in the Vicsek model, a classical model of self-propelled particles.
motivation: Understanding how limited and offset sensory information influences group coordination in biological and robotic swarms.
method: Agent-based simulations of the two-dimensional Vicsek model with a parameter controlling the angular offset of each agent's visual field.
result: The visual field offset significantly alters the onset and nature of collective motion, leading to novel phases not present in the standard Vicsek model.
conclusion: Visual field offset is a crucial parameter for collective behavior, with implications for designing robotic swarms and interpreting biological systems.

result: Optimized shock timing enhances fuel compression and ignition performance.

authors: Chao-Sheng Li, Shun-Jie Wu, Rong-Rong Cai, And Li-Zhi Zhang

motivation: Understanding the origin of circular dichroism in photoelectron angular distributions (CDAD) from achiral molecules, which can arise from experimental geometry or final-state scattering effects.

motivation: Microplastic fibers are a major pollutant in the ocean, but their vertical distribution and residence time at the sea surface are poorly understood, which affects their environmental impact.
method: The authors combine field measurements of fiber length distributions at the sea surface and at 5 m depth with a theoretical model of fiber rise velocity and turbulent mixing.
result: They observe a higher ratio of long to short fibers at the surface than at depth, indicating a surface-enrichment effect that depends on fiber length.
conclusion: The sea surface selectively retains longer microfibers, which has implications for their transport, degradation, and ecological effects.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: A review of hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: To understand strong interaction (QCD) through charmonium decays and search for new hadrons.
method: Review of experimental results from BaBar, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII on hadron production in e+e- collisions.
result: Summarizes current progress and highlights BESIII's leading role in high-precision measurements.
conclusion: Hadron spectroscopy in charm meson pairs provides crucial insights into QCD, with BESIII advancing the field.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of planetary radar observations at Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: To summarize the scientific legacy of the Arecibo planetary radar system after its upgrade.
method: Review of radar techniques and key observations of planets, moons, and asteroids.
result: Highlights the unique subsurface and surface insights provided by radar, aiding in situ exploration.
conclusion: Arecibo radar was a uniquely sensitive instrument that significantly advanced planetary science.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A historical review of the Arecibo radio telescope's contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To document the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory and its scientific impact over five decades.
method: Historical narrative and summary of key scientific results from Arecibo's upgrades and observations.
result: Arecibo made major contributions to pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave detection.
conclusion: Arecibo's unique capabilities and upgrades enabled groundbreaking discoveries in radio astronomy.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews advances in geospace science using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: To summarize key scientific contributions from the Arecibo Observatory in upper atmosphere and ionospheric research.
method: Review of incoherent scatter radar technique and results from Arecibo's radar, lidar, and optical instruments.
result: Highlights advances in plasma physics, space weather, metal layers, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in geospace research, but the paper is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: The rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is poorly understood; controlled experiments are needed.
method: The paper synthesizes experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of convection-cloud chambers that reproduce key cloud microphysics.
result: Convection-cloud chambers can generate turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation, bridging laboratory and atmospheric scales.
conclusion: These chambers offer a promising platform to address the precipitation bottleneck, but further work is needed to fully connect lab results to atmospheric clouds.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection in multimessenger astronomy.
motivation: Core collapse supernovae are rare events that provide unique insights into stellar physics and neutron star formation; detecting gravitational waves alongside photons and neutrinos would enable multimessenger studies.
method: The paper summarizes recent progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection methods and parameter estimation for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: It presents the latest predictions for gravitational wave signatures from neutrino-driven core collapse supernovae and outlines strategies for multimessenger observation.
conclusion: A Galactic supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, and current detectors are poised to extract physical parameters from the gravitational wave signal.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a tension between the dipole in the cosmic microwave background and that in large-scale structure, challenging the cosmological principle.
motivation: To test the foundational cosmological principle of isotropy and homogeneity by comparing the dipole in galaxy/quasar catalogs with the CMB dipole.
method: Analysis of large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in their distribution, and comparison with the CMB dipole interpreted as due to peculiar motion.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The anomaly may challenge the standard ΛCDM model and motivate further investigation into systematic biases or new physics.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: A review of astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their observational signatures.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and test self-interacting dark matter scenarios using astrophysical observations.
method: Review of theoretical models and observational constraints from galaxies to large-scale structures, including simulations and data analysis.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and outlines future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable candidate, but more precise astrophysical tests are needed to distinguish it from other models.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental constraints and discovery potential.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, but recent LHC results have constrained its parameter space, motivating a survey of viable models and future search strategies.
method: The authors review theoretical models and experimental searches, and project discovery potential for the HL-LHC across multiple channels.
result: The paper provides an overview of current constraints and outlines scenarios where supersymmetry could still be discovered at the HL-LHC.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable in certain regions, and the HL-LHC offers significant discovery potential for well-motivated models.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion reactions and their diagnostics.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar properties like luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The review summarizes theoretical models and experimental data from the last decade on nuclear reaction rates, plasma physics, and atomic effects in the solar interior.
result: Updated reaction rates and improved models for the solar fusion network are presented, along with comparisons to neutrino and helioseismic observations.
conclusion: The new data and theory refine our understanding of solar fusion, but the paper is purely astrophysical and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This review covers the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, focusing on turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding gas bubble dynamics is important for natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The paper is a review summarizing key advances over the past 20 years, discussing topics such as added mass, deformable surfaces, turbulence, and rheology.
result: The review highlights the complex behavior of bubbles and provides insights for modeling two-phase flow systems.
conclusion: The paper offers a comprehensive overview of bubble dynamics but has no relevance to the user's research interests.

title: Using Gravitational Waves To See The First Second Of The Universe
abstract:
Author(s): Rishav Roshan and Graham White

Gravitational waves open a unique window on the earliest times in cosmology because the dense primordial plasma, impenetrable to light or neutrinos, is transparent to gravitational waves up to the instant of the birth of the Universe. This review discusses the possible signals from the phase transitions, topological defects, and other cosmological sources, as well as a range of strategies for detection of the stochastic gravitational waves produced by the earliest events in the history of the Universe.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015001] Published Wed Jan 08, 2025.
tldr: A review of gravitational wave signals from the early universe, focusing on phase transitions and topological defects.
motivation: To explore how gravitational waves can probe the first second of the universe, which is opaque to electromagnetic radiation.
method: Review of theoretical models for gravitational wave production from cosmological sources and detection strategies.
result: Summarizes potential signals from phase transitions, topological defects, and other early-universe phenomena.
conclusion: Gravitational waves offer a unique window into the early universe, but detection requires future observatories.

title: Orthogonal Phase Modulation And Lissajous Mode Decoupling In Light-induced Thermoelastic Spectroscopy For Real-time Multi-component Gas Sensing
authors: Hanxu Ma, Shunda Qiao, Ying He, Haiyue Sun And Yufei Ma
abstract: This paper proposed an optical detection mechanism that utilized orthogonal phase modulation (OPM) and Lissajous mode decoupling within a light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy (LITES) sensor for the first time, enabling real-time multi-component gas sensing. By establishing a two-dimensional forced vibration model of a quartz tuning fork (QTF) under dual-path OPM, it revealed the vibration mode coupling mechanism induced by non-ideal phase and amplitude conditions, thereby providing a theoretical basis and optimization pathway for suppressing channel crosstalk. In the OPM-LITES sensor, two continuous-wave distributed feedback lasers were modulated by sinusoidal waves with the same frequency (f0/2, where f0 is the resonant frequency of the QTF) but a phase difference of 45°. The combined beam, after wavelength division multiplexing, co-excited the self-designed low-frequency QTF. The piezoelectric signal generated by the QTF underwent orthogonal demodulation via a lock-in amplifier (LIA). The concentration information for the two gases was independently retrieved from the decoupled X-component and Y-component of the LIA. Experimental results demonstrated that the OPM-LITES sensor exhibited excellent linear responses to both methane (CH4) and acetylene (C2H2), with average relative systematic errors of 0.54% and 0.79%, and maximum relative errors of 1.72% and 1.38%, respectively. Allan deviation analysis indicated that the minimum detection limits (MDLs) for CH4 and C2H2 reached 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, with normalized noise-equivalent absorption coefficients of 5.09 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2 and 6.18 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2, respectively. This study not only provided a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection but also established a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling and signal processing in spectroscopic sensing.
tldr: This paper presents a novel optical gas sensing technique using orthogonal phase modulation and Lissajous mode decoupling in light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy for real-time multi-component gas detection.
motivation: Real-time multi-component gas sensing is important for environmental monitoring and industrial safety, but existing methods suffer from channel crosstalk and complexity.
method: Two lasers are modulated with same frequency but 45° phase difference, co-excite a quartz tuning fork, and the piezoelectric signal is orthogonally demodulated to retrieve two gas concentrations independently.
result: The sensor achieves linear responses for CH4 and C2H2 with low systematic errors (0.54% and 0.79%) and detection limits of 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, respectively.
conclusion: The proposed OPM-LITES sensor provides a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection with a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling.

motivation: Understanding how bacterial pathogens adapt to varying viscosity in host environments is important for infection biology.

tldr: A generative model for predicting atomic packing in protein voids, applied to computational protein design.
motivation: Improve computational protein design by accurately modeling atomic packing in protein voids to enable specific protein–protein and protein–drug interactions.

tldr: This paper describes the engineering of a ribozyme with increased GTP turnover, relevant to prebiotic RNA self-replication.
motivation: To understand how early life could have used catalytic RNAs for self-replication, requiring efficient RNA polymerization from activated nucleotides.

result: The engineered ribozyme exhibits significantly increased GTP turnover compared to previous variants.
conclusion: The work advances our understanding of ribozyme evolution and the potential for RNA-based self-replication in prebiotic chemistry.

SignificanceTip links gate mechanotransduction channels in cochlear hair cells and have been proposed to be the gating springs for the transduction channel. The ultrastructure of the tip link remains not well defined. Here we have used cryo-electron ...
tldr: This paper uses cryo-electron microscopy to determine the structure of the Pcdh15 protein, revealing a right-handed double-helix dimer architecture relevant to mechanotransduction in hair cells.
motivation: The ultrastructure of the tip link, which gates mechanotransduction channels in cochlear hair cells, is not well defined. Understanding its structure is crucial for elucidating the mechanism of hearing.
method: The authors employed cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to image the Pcdh15 protein and reconstructed its three-dimensional structure.
result: They found that Pcdh15 forms a right-handed double-helix dimer, providing a structural basis for its role as a gating spring in mechanotransduction.
conclusion: The structural insights advance the understanding of tip link architecture and its function in hearing, but the work is purely structural biology with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

tldr: This paper investigates the role of Rnf126 in peroxisome elimination during hypoxia-driven dedifferentiation of hepatocellular carcinoma cells, proposing a redifferentiation therapy strategy.
motivation: Cancer cell dedifferentiation is a hallmark of malignancy and a therapeutic challenge; understanding the molecular mechanisms could lead to new treatments.
method: The study uses molecular biology techniques to show that hypoxia induces peroxisome degradation via Rnf126, and tests redifferentiation therapy in HCC models.
result: Rnf126 acts as a fate switch by eliminating peroxisomes, and targeting this pathway can promote redifferentiation of cancer cells.
conclusion: Rnf126-mediated peroxisome removal is a key step in HCC dedifferentiation, and its inhibition may enable redifferentiation therapy.

tldr: This paper investigates the role of Drp1-driven mitochondrial fragmentation in scleral tissue as a mechanism promoting myopia development.
motivation: To understand the molecular mechanisms underlying scleral collagen reduction, which is a key factor in ocular axial elongation and myopia.

motivation: Understanding how metabolic cues regulate blood cell production is important for immunology, but the molecular sensors are unknown.
